newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: WTO Cuba panel combines diplomat, trade experts.
newsitem.headline: WTO Cuba panel combines diplomat, trade experts.

text.p: The three members of the World Trade Organisation panel appointed on Thursday to look into the EU-U.S. row over investment in Cuba combine decades of experience in international trade and diplomacy.
The following are brief sketches of their careers:

ARTHUR DUNKEL - A 64-year-old multi-lingual Swiss economist, he served as Director-General of the old General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) from 1980-1993. In that role over a key period for the global trading system, he won a reputation as a quiet, careful and meticulous "details man" and a conciliator.

But when a figure with a higher international profile and personal ebullience was needed in 1993 to force governments to concentrate on wrapping up the long-running Uruguay Round negotiations, the retiring Dunkel stepped aside and was replaced by Irishman Peter Sutherland.

Since then, he has worked as economics professor at the universities of Geneva and Fribourg and is chairman of the Paris-based International Chamber of Commerce's Commission on International Trade and Investment Policy.

TOMMY KOH - One of South-East Asia's best-known figures on the international diplomatic stage with long, first-hand experience of the United States, he is currently ambassador-at- large for Singapore's Foreign Ministry. Born in 1937, he became the island-state's permanent representative to the United Nations in New York at the age of 29 in 1968, holding the post until 1971, and then taking it again for a decade from 1974-84, chairing the U.N. General Assembly.

In 1981-82, he presided over the Third U.N. Conference on the Law of the Sea, then served as Singapore's ambassador to the United States from 1984-90, and from 1900-92 played a key role in organising the 1992 U.N. Conference on Environment and Development in Rio de Janeiro, the "Earth Summit".
He holds a Master's degree in law from Harvard University and a doctorate in law from Yale as well as a diploma in criminology from Britain's Cambridge University.

EDWARD WOODFIELD - An economist by training born in in 1936, he was New Zealand's chief international trade negotiator from 1981-89 at a time when the country was breaking away from a rigid, protected market to become what the WTO recently hailed as one of the world's most open trading states.

He led his government's delegations to major international conferences on trade and economic issues, including to the negotiations in the GATT's Tokyo and Uruguay Rounds. He served as High Commissioner to Australia from 1989-94.

Since 1994, he has worked as an independent consultant, carrying out commissions for New Zealand's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade including provision of policy advice on trazde policy to Oman, Cambodia, Laos and Vietnam who are alll hoping to join the WTO.
